utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. And good afternoon to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, temporarily Alexis Demirdjian, and Crispian Smith, temporarily being to deal with the disclosure arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence this afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Dragan Krgovic and Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we do anything else, because I don't trust myself not to forget it, we would alert the parties that after -- when we take the summer recess in this case - and the reason why we're doing it this afternoon is because this would be -- is being done contemporaneously with a like announcement being made elsewhere - when we take the summer adjournment in this -- in the present case, we will not be in a position to resume the hearings until the week beginning the 29th of August because of the decisions, and counsel would be aware of the heavy e-mail traffic that has gone on for the past several weeks now, about balancing, sharing the time, between this case and the case of Haradinaj. The other matters is, there's a very brief ruling which the Chamber has to deliver. And it is dealing with the motion by the Stanisic Defence to compel the Prosecution to comply with Rule 66(B). And the -- upon examination of the requests from the counsel for Stanisic, the Chamber finds that they fall far short of meeting the conditions required in Rule 66(B) of the Rules. And pursuant to Rule 54 and 66(B), the Chamber denies the motion. That is the oral decision. There is a written decision which is in the process of being prepared and which we expect to issue shortly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, just before Mr. Zecevic raises the matters he wants to raise, can I go back to the sitting arrangements and ask whether Your Honours are able to tell us whether the suggestion I think that was made by all parties to the various cases, namely that it will be two weeks on one case and two weeks on another, is what's going to be accepted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. That is the -- I don't have with me the projection through to the end of the year, but I do remember the beginning. We would begin after the summer recess with the other case, and Stanisic and Zupljanin will pick up on the 29th of August, and thereafter it will alternate as counsel have -- in two-week periods. That seems, from the input of all of the interested parties, the most practical way of dealing with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Your Honours. That's -- that's very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I do have a comment on that, because Your Honours mentioned that that seems to be the case, from the input of all the interested parties, the most practical way of dealing with that. Your Honours, I'm pretty sure that the Trial Chamber is aware of the fact that we never responded to that mail because, Your Honours, we required first and foremost to consult the Office of Legal Aid before we can provide the answer to the Trial Chamber, and it's been going for some time with the OLAD and the Registry about that and it creates a significant problem from the point of -- from the point of Defence if it's two-weeks' breaks. And I'm not sure because we still don't have a feedback from OLAD about what is their position going to be in respect to our obligations as appointees by the OLAD. So in that respect I ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. -- I would only say, because it is partly confidential, that OLAD has provisionally concretized a view. The problems which these -- running these cases simultaneously create do not admit of easy solutions, and the -- where we are now in terms of the way forward is not chiselled in stone. And one of the reasons why the -- I made the announcement that I did is so that if there are any difficulties which counsel or the parties have which are not yet apparent to the Judges, that no doubt you would make it known and we would see where we go. So inasmuch as a decision had to be made, particularly in terms of the other case, for the ancillary reasons connected with starting a case, that is where we are, and we would see where further discussions and further thoughts place us in the weeks to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours. I'm sorry, but we were not informed by OLAD that -- of their position, and that is why I brought this to the attention of the Judges. Your Honours, I announced that I have a quick submission and -- well, rather quick. It will depend what Your Honours think about that. And I would like to raise a few matters which are a concern, a grave concern, for the Defence. But let me try with the relief that we are seeking, and I hope I will not shock the Trial Chamber with the relief we are seeking. Your Honours, we are asking the adjournment until next Thursday in presentation of our Defence case, and the reasons are the following: First of all, we would like to see the compliance motion because -- the decision of the Trial Chamber on our motion for compliance of the Office of the Prosecutor based on 66(B) because we have -- we think it goes to the matter of utmost importance for the Defence which is the fairness of the proceedings. Therefore, we will be -- I hope we will be in a position do that within a week time. That would be one of the reasons. The second reason, Your Honours, is the fact that in last seven days we received from the Office of the Prosecutor 132 documents signed by Mr. Mico Stanisic which have never ever been disclosed to us before. Now, apparently the Office of the Prosecutor felt that these documents, which were in their possession quite some time, do not meet the requirements of Rule 68 or that are irrelevant in this case, however, as I had a very short time to get myself acquainted with some of the documents, we do not share that view. And, Your Honours, with all due respect, we need definitely some time to analyse these documents and see whether we can introduce some of these documents in our Defence case. On top of it, we just recently made a finding in the electronic disclosure system of a whole batch of CSB Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Zecevic, when you say 132 documents, should we be thinking of 132 pages or 132 by an average of, say, multiplied by five or three or whatnot; how much paper are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, it --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, thank you very much, but let me finish. It is -- most of them are one single-page document, so I think we are talking about roughly 132 to 140 pages altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The second thing, as I said, is the findings of the batch of documents of CSB Sarajevo. Those documents are -- those documents have never ever appeared before in all our searches of EDS, but that's only understandable knowing the electronic glitches that we have in that system. Now, we are not sure how many documents are there, but so far we've been -- it's a number of documents. And since our next witness is actually talking about the CSB Sarajevo for the relevant period of -- for the indictment, we would need to review that batch as well. The fourth reason is the fact that we intend to shorten our witness list. When I say that, I -- we still have four witnesses left on our original 65 ter list. We intend to drop two of the witnesses from that list. But then there is a number of documents which we wanted to introduce through these witnesses, and we would like to be able to be given the opportunity to consult the remaining two witnesses whether any of the documents came within their knowledge or if they can comment on these documents so we can perhaps introduce them through the remaining two witnesses. And, well, Your Honours, that's basically my submission. I don't want to -- I can go at length about any of these points, but I'm happy to answer any question if the Trial Chamber would have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And to bring you back to where you started, your application is such that the four days, is it, between now and Thursday would put you in a position to deal with these issues; that's what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we don't have any witnesses for one day, so Mr. -- our next witness has not yet arrived, so therefore tomorrow was anyhow -- we would have been adjourned. But -- and Monday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- is a holiday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- is a holiday. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That's why I counted four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So therefore we are asking for two days -- well, yes, two days next week in order to be able to deal with these issues, yes. Tuesday and Wednesday, so we start --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, only two days. Two days, really. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the first thing to be said is, as I explained yesterday, at no stage did the Defence seek your leave not to call the next witness tomorrow. Although, having said that, and as Your Honours know, a witness that should have lasted no more, top whack, than six hours in cross-examination because of his complete and utter inability to answer questions is still here and, if he goes on like this, may well be here tomorrow, so that's one matter. The second matter is this: Your Honours, we do dispute that with the exception of three documents, which we enumerate for the Defence, any of the documents that we gave them addressed to, or signed by, Stanisic as a result of the very, very late 66(B) request are relevant. Can I give you an example, Your Honours, of the one-page documents that have been disclosed because of the request. A document about a request for the registration of a Golf. A document about confirmation of the ownership of the vehicle. A document asking for the costs of reparation. Well, Your Honour, I don't know why Mr. Zecevic is on his feet, because I'm now answering.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, but I specifically said that I can go at length about -- if we are going to talk about the specific documents, I can go at length about that. And I don't think it's fair that Ms. Korner is now using the exact documents addressing my general request. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I suppose that the -- and, of course, I don't have it in front of me, but when the Defence would have requested all documents signed by the Accused Stanisic, I assume that the Prosecution would have been entitled to exclude from that, for instance, if the minister had made a requisition for paper clips. So I think that that is where Ms. Korner is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I say, I'm dealing with the request. And part of it is the desire to go through these documents, which would take, I would imagine, something like half an hour. We've identified three, ourselves, that personally if we'd known about them we would have used, ourselves, but which are relevant and more. Your Honours, the difficulty is this, and Your Honours have made it clear that we're not going to be able to sit full time on this case once the Haradinaj case starts. And although it may well be, and almost certainly will be, the fact that Mr. Stanisic's case has finished before the -- well, it will have finished before the recess, on the face of it, we should be using such court time as we have available to us before the other case starts. That's what we say should be happening. As regards the question of witnesses, we would like to know, please, which witnesses are not going to be called because we've already spent some time preparing for witnesses and doing a lot of unnecessary work on witnesses we're now told won't be coming. So we'd like to be told, please, which are the two witnesses who the Defence are now no longer proposing to call, although I can make a pretty good guess, I think. Your Honours, as regards the adjournment, our view is, as I say, that, A, leave should have been asked not to have the witness here to start tomorrow, and, B, that the case should go on and use the time available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, anything in reply? I seem to recall that we would have cautioned counsel against approaching this matter of number of witnesses and the time of seeing it as a sort of bank from which they could make deposits and withdrawals as need be. You have -- of course, you have an outside number of hours within which to complete your case, but that apart, I'm not sure that your strongest point is that you would -- by -- because you would not be calling two other witnesses, that that is a reason, sufficient reason, to -- or one of the reasons that would support your argument. But anything else in reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I discussed with Ms. Korner about the Friday, and it's probably that she missed that I told her that we don't have a witness before coming Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Forget about Friday. I'm talking about the Tuesday and Wednesday, the two days that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but, Your Honours, I'm not -- I just wanted to inform the Trial Chamber that that is our intention. We still haven't decided but we intend to decide today or over the weekend about the two witnesses that we are going to drop off our list. However, the point, Your Honours, is the following: There is a number of documents that we intended to show to these witnesses. Now, these documents were never shown to the other witnesses and there is -- that's one of the reasons why we need the additional time to prepare that, with all the other reasons which I already stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry, but either Mr. Zecevic is dropping the witnesses, in which case he has to show the documents, or he's not. And I would ask Your Honours to order that he tells us today who he is not calling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Chamber appreciates that this is a matter in which it has to rule urgently. But in the circumstances, we would require the witness to be re-called to the stand and we will discuss this during a break and give our ruling in the course of this afternoon's sitting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're on scheduling and housekeeping matters, first of all, could we ask Your Honours to order that the Zupljanin Defence give us a batting order, in other words, the order in which they'll be calling their witnesses, as we appear to be pretty close to the beginning of their case, even closer by the sound of it. The other matter is this: That on - I've forgotten what day it was - thank you, 2nd of June, Mr. Hannis cross-examined Mr. Andan on some photographs of Dusko Malovic's Group and it was agreed that if photographs were taken from the package which weren't relevant, the document -- sorry, which was MFI'd, could have the MFI status lifted. It's P2346. A document has been prepared which only contains the photographs that Andan identified, so could we ask that that document be numbered 20145.01.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, sorry, I read out the wrong number, that's why I got confused myself, as ever, with these numbers. We'd like P2346, the 65 ter instead of being 20145 will be 20145.01. And can we have the MFI status lifted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry, I don't quite understand what Ms. Korner is doing with these numbers. But in any case, I believe P2346 should be de-MFI'd after it's uploaded with the photographs that I agreed and we didn't object. However, Your Honours, before that is done, we would like to be given a copy of the -- these -- of this new exhibit that is going to be so we know what we are -- what we are getting admitted into documents. The actual pictures.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's actually already been uploaded into e-court, so the pictures are available for Mr. Zecevic to look at them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the MFI qualification is removed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So could the usher please escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just checked the document, and it still has 41 pages and all the irrelevant documents. I just opened it right now. 2346, MFI.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, if I may, the new document has been released at 65 ter 20145.01, and that contains only nine pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Will that new document be given the -- now, the problem is the following: We are taking the MFI from the document in e-court, and the document in e-court, 2-whatever-6436, is the 41-pages document. We are not dealing with the 65 ter numbers in the e-court. If it's a document which has been de-MFI'd, it should be the only five or six pictures and not the whole document in e-court, that's my problem.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, since the order has been made a couple of minutes ago, the document will be replaced within the next couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is precisely why I asked that the Office of the Prosecutor should have sent us the courtesy copy before they actually offered it to be de-MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, before -- good afternoon to you. I remind you you're still on your oath. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, Mr. Orasanin, yesterday, to answer one single simply question, you took up 24 lines of transcript and didn't answer the question. I would like, in a rather hopeless fashion, I agree, to ask you today, so that we can finish, to answer questions "yes" or "no" or "I don't know," and only if it is absolutely vital to give any further explanation. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, when we broke off yesterday, we were dealing with matters relating to appointments, and I want to move -- by the minister, I should say. But I want to move to what you said about Bijeljina and that was on the first day of your testimony, at page 21886. And I think you told the Court that you dropped in at Bijeljina; is that correct? Just let me find the right part. Yes. Yes, Mr. Cvijetic said we should move on to Brcko and Bijeljina, and you told him that you hadn't planned to be in Bijeljina but you went to the police station, none of the chiefs were there, "we found the chief of legal affairs who had nothing to do with the operatives." Now, before I spend any time showing you documents from Bijeljina, are you saying that you did any kind of an inspection in Bijeljina or simply that you passed through it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated that we were going to Brcko, and Bijeljina was on the way. We visited Brcko and on our way back we stopped at Bijeljina. We didn't find Chief Jesuric there, but we found the chief of the administration and legal department, Mr. Grkinic, and we called on him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, stop there. Simple question: Did you do any kind of inspection or did you just go through it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We called at the station and stayed awhile with Grkinic. We had coffee with the chief of the administrative and legal department at the Bijeljina CSB or, actually, the Bijeljina SJB which had been set up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So the answer to the question is no, you did not do any inspection or visit it formally; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as you entered the building, by virtue of that fact and by -- as a consequence of spending time with one of the managers, we did some work. But we didn't speak with any operatives, the heads of the police, or the crime prevention service. That's the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, because we -- I think the simplest thing is to show you a document, please, which is 20161, tab 4B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could I -- Mr. Orasanin, could I, in the meantime, ask how long that visit took?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now we're back to the matter that you seem to be disputing, that certainly in April and May Mr. Jesuric was chief of the CSB. It's addressed to the security -- sorry, sent by the Security Services Centre Bijeljina and the Public Security Station Bijeljina, Ministry of the Interior, to the minister and deputy minister that -- in the Security Services Centre in Bijeljina. The security station situation has not changed, the situation in Bijeljina is normal, et cetera, et cetera, dated the 22nd of April, 1992. When you went and visited in May, was the situation in Bijeljina normal?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were doing some work there but there were some problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. What were the problems that were identified to you by whoever you spoke to there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know but I can't remember now whether it was that period or later because the MUP had moved to Bijeljina, and that's why I'm a bit confused, because there were some groups there. I remember that there was an attack on the police station. If that was a month later or when exactly, that's my confusion with regard to what I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, Mr. Orasanin, I just want to make this clear: Are you disputing that for some period, and I fully understand that there were a number of changes of CSB chiefs in Bijeljina, Mr. Jesuric was chief of the CSB? Or if you don't know one way or the other, then please say, "I do not know."

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the confusion yesterday is logical. I do know, after all, how it should be. The organisation of CSBs or the MUP is always parallel to that of the judiciary, namely the courts. Wherever there are district courts, there are centres. And in early May, I said yesterday that I had documents with the organisation of district courts, where district courts and prosecutor's offices are set up in Banja Luka, Doboj, Bijeljina, Sarajevo, and Trebinje, and the organisation of CSBs was parallel. There was a CSB in Bijeljina. I was carrying some documents and those were instructions of the Presidency and instructions on the setting up of courts and prosecutor's offices. We carried them with us to the field and we distributed them to police stations for them to have. It was early May. I have those documents even now somewhere. I can find them. And that's the dilemma. And there certainly was a CSB in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because -- because that was the organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Stop. Honestly, I really think you're not listening to the question. The question was: Do you dispute - I hope that's clear in translation - that Mr. Jesuric, for a period, was chief of the CSB in Bijeljina? That's the only question.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was chief of the Bijeljina SJB. And when the centre was set up, well, it's logical, but I can't remember now because they were in the same building.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, in that case, as this is suddenly, after two years of trial, become an issue, I'm going to ask that this document now be marked and admitted as evidence on the face of this document that Mr. Jesuric was chief of the CSB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic? Mr. Cvijetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have our usual objection to this document and to the introduction of documents at this stage of cross-examination. I wish to reiterate that it's still our position that this document cannot be tendered now. I have already said so yesterday when I referred to the standards set in the Prlic case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I've made it clear: Nobody could have anticipated that suddenly, for no good reason that I can see, this witness has chosen to dispute that Mr. Jesuric was chief of the CSB. And, Your Honour, it's obviously important that if we have documents that have -- otherwise really are of no relevance whatsoever, that show that he was, we should be allowed to enter them into evidence at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, could you remind me the tab number, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's tab 4B. Yes, 4B.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I may just comment, Your Honours, I'm sorry that I'm interrupting, but this sounds to me like a document testing the credibility of the witness. If that is the purpose of this document, then we say we don't have a problem admitting this document. But if this document is to show something else, Ms. Korner produced -- or the Office of the Prosecutor, Your Honours, at the very beginning of the case, produced the huge maps explaining the structure of the MUP, so they knew that they have to prove that these persons were holding those positions, so, therefore, saying that they were not aware that this might be an issue in the case is, with all due respect, not true, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's perfectly true because admitted into evidence are pretty pictures of the CSB with those pretty men which say under it, if it I can just get my copy, and nobody has ever suggested to us it is the obligation of the Defence, when they know that we're putting documents in as truth of their contents, if they dispute it, to say so. This document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Korner, against that background, and the document you referred to being already in evidence, isn't it -- I don't understand the present exchange between yourself and the witness on the stand to make that a fact in issue, and, therefore, wouldn't it be -- isn't the admission of this limited to his credibility and therefore --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I think I'm going mad actually slightly. This whole thing has been reversed. We have proved our case. It is the obligation of the Defence to put the case. If it is the Defence case that they challenge that Mr. Jesuric, for a short period of time -- and you'll see, Your Honours, if you look at the diagram, that there were huge numbers of changes. It's P881.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I know I tend to have the -- I have a tendency to be elliptical in my speech, but basically I'm agreeing with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, but I think it's incumbent upon the Defence to make it clear that is not their case, that Mr. Jesuric was not at some stage chief of the CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But, Your Honours, we never said so. We never said so. We never said that we are challenging that fact. It concerns the fresh evidence that Ms. Korner wants to introduce through this witness. We say she can't do that; she has to explain according to the standard which this Trial Chamber adopted. If she wants to introduce the new evidence, she has to provide an explanation. And that is the point. But if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, need we confuse ourselves by going down that road? If in fact there is no issue as to whether Mr. Jesuric was chief of CSB security, and the only point is what has arisen in cross-examination out of the mouth of this witness, [indiscernible] even a question of credibility. So need we exercise ourselves about --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But that is precisely what I said, Your Honours. I said if it goes for the credibility of the witness, we do not object. Now, but then Ms. Korner went further on that. That's my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the document is admitted and we move on.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2352, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Brcko, Mr. Orasanin. So again you say Brcko, according to you at page 21888, the crime service wasn't organised, that -- well, actually, you don't say much except you had a flat tyre. Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just so that we don't have any discussion about Brcko, can we have a look, please, at 10B, which is 20166, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you agree that's a list of salaries for the Brcko Police in the period from the 1st of May to 31st of May?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the same case as in the stations we looked at previously.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Last page in each, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Apparently Brcko in May had some 56 police officers working there, so, would you agree, fully functioning police station?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was speaking about this, perhaps I can explain additionally, yesterday and the day before about these payrolls. When we went out in the field, to my mind this was not the real situation. I think that some names are fictitious. This should be examined in detail. I know some police officers who came to see me and they had been in Belgrade for several months and then they were put on the list as of early April and they had only arrived in July. It isn't really the payrolls that [indiscernible] to me when I went to the stations but only the lists in accordance with the rule book on internal organisation. I may not be competent to speak about this, but we spoke about a case yesterday. Two police officers who had arrived later but were retroactively put on the list as being there since early April but they had only come in May or July respectively. One's name is Branko Glamocic [phoen] and the other was Rajko something. And there were dozens of such cases. In Brcko I didn't see these people. I didn't see any in Skelani either. To my mind, this is all fictitious. We were the first team that went to the field for the MUP -- or from the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Tell us exactly how long you carried out your, in inverted commas, visit in Brcko, would you, Mr. Orasanin?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must be honest because I'm such a man. I said that our visits were such that we wanted to do something and make a snap-shot of the situation, see how people worked there. And we wanted them to see us because we were the first who had arrived there. And we found a chaotic situation. We were in Brcko for something over an hour. We went to the police station, found the duty officer, and I remember this man Gavrilovic, I think that his first name is Pero, he came to meet us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No -- stop. You told us all this. I don't want to hear it again, please. You were there for one hour. Right. You don't accept the evidence of the payrolls. Have a look at one other document, then, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which is, sorry, 13A, which is ... oh, it's a Defence document, 1D547.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is from Brcko, minutes of the meeting of the specialist board of the Serb SJB held on the 2nd of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we go, please, to the last page in both B/C/S and English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Recognise the names of Mr. Veselic and Mr. Lugonjic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we go, please, to the third page in English and it's the fourth page in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The earlier part deals with the jobs that would be done by the various officials. "Considering the fact that policemen at this moment are engaged in providing physical security for working organisations and other vital facilities on the territory of the municipality, Brcko SJB had agreed with the War Presidency to have our forces withdrawn. In accordance with this agreement, the number of personnel at the police station will be increased and consequently the normal functioning of the SJB will be ensured, meaning shift patrols in the field. Communication with policemen through USW devices, all available radio equipment will be checked and used." Next heading, "Crime." "The affairs and task of the field of crime have been functioning from the very division, i.e., the establishing of the Brcko Serb SJB." All right. Do you accept that you could be wrong in the conclusion you drew in your brief one-hour visit to Brcko about the functioning of Brcko SJB during the second half of May or thereabouts?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that during that hour we spent there we mostly dealt with the jobs of the uniformed police, and I was there to see about crime enforcement. I met Gavrilovic, who was in charge of crime enforcement. And these are my duties with regard to the crime prevention service. That's why I'm not familiar with the jobs of the uniformed police. And we didn't have time there because we were chased away by sniper fire. That's the essence. We didn't really work there, that's why it was such a short visit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. That will do. All right. Now I want to deal with the -- your evidence about the fact that various stations did not belong to -- were not allocated to any CSBs. We dealt already with what you had to say about Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have a look, please, at a document -- Now, Your Honours, this has not been translated because it's one of these financial documents, but we weren't aware that there was going to be this kind of evidence. So it will have to come up in B/C/S only, and obviously if I wanted to have it admitted as an exhibit, we'd have to get a translation. But it's a very simple point I want to make. Could we have, please, on the screen the document which is at tab 7.1, which has been given the number 20168.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, is that a document dated the 7th of May, 1992, and does it come from what is said to be the CSB Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And does that show the --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just a moment, please. From the witness's testimony so far, we have been able to conclude that while he was affiliated with the Ministry of the Interior, he did not carry out any inspections in Trebinje in the Security Services Centre there. So I suppose he cannot speak to the contents of the document because he probably never saw the document before nor he inspected the situation there, and he also did not testify -- he did not tell us anything about that particular Security Services Centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this has got nothing to do with any inspections that he did. This is to do with whether what he called the eastern municipalities or SJBs were affiliated to any CSBs, and that's the matter I'm dealing with. I'm showing him this document, and I'm going to ask him if he still wants to adhere to the evidence he gave about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, because we haven't got a translation, could you just read out, if you can, and if you can't I'll give you a hard copy, what the -- after we can -- what the first line says after the date. Could you read it out in your language. Perhaps we could highlight that part for him if he is having difficulty. What does that say, please? Read it out.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then could you read, please, the next few lines.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Here enclosed please find lists of employees who are present at the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and who are employed in public security stations of the Security Services Centre in Trebinje."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Right. Can we just deal, please, then, with -- well, perhaps we can deal fairly quickly with which stations did belong to it. What's the first station there? Just read it out, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Srecko, Djeric.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Not the name, the name of the station.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trebinje. Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go on, please, to page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What's the station at the top there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the Gacko Public Security Station.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next one.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljubinje SJB.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: One below.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bileca SJB.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, there's so many of them. Perhaps if we just go to page 6 to identify the one I want to identify. Page 6, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What is that one in the middle?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Visegrad SJB.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Wasn't that one of the SJBs you said didn't belong to any CSB?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I spoke about my visit to Visegrad, Foca, Rudo, I said that they were left in the cold, that they had not received any assistance. We were the only ones who came. It was an obligation of the CSB to help those stations, but we were the only ones who arrived from the Ministry of the Interior to get stock of their situation. This is what we covered in our report. That's what I meant when I said that they were not covered, that in organisational terms they were left out in the cold. As for the legality of the whole thing, I would say that you can put anything on paper. But there, on the ground, they all complained that nobody had visited them before September 1992 when we arrived in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I am -- I did not deal with organisation. We performed our duties and we realised that there were some negative things at stake in terms of the operation of the SJB in Trebinje because nobody had arrived to visit them for five or six months before we arrived, although it was their duty to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, the CSB Trebinje had enough, if you like - what's the word you used? - oversight over them or - sorry, trying to find the word you used - assistance to at least get their payment organised, hadn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Your Honours. How is the witness supposed to know that? What is the foundation on which Ms. Korner concludes that there were enough operatives, there were enough employees who could have carried out that task?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's not -- Mr. Cvijetic is picking up problems from Mr. Orasanin. That's not the question I asked. The question I put to Mr. Orasanin is that they had enough involvement to arrange for the payment, judging by this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would you agree with that, Mr. Orasanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, this is Mr. Cvijetic's witness. We cannot have people bobbing up and down like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand fully, but there is a problem obviously with the translation because Mr. Cvijetic got obviously the different question. The point, I'm trying to assist. If don't want me to assist, I will not. And I'm not asking to say anything. The point of matter is, Your Honours, Ms. Korner is basing her document on the document she can't read, and this document doesn't have anything to do with the payments. That's the point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, I had Mr. Orasanin read out the beginning of the document so we could see what it was about. "... please find lists of employees who are present at the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic ... who are employed in public security stations of the Security Services Centre in Trebinje." Yes, I take the point. It's not exactly a financial document. It comes from a financial thing but it's not exactly. I'm told -- just a moment. Can we go to the -- sorry, can we go to the very end of the document, I think that may be why I thought they were payment. To do with -- ah, that's right. Your Honours, I'm sorry, I'd forgotten that attached to the end of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you agree that's a payment slip of some kind, Mr. Orasanin?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order issued to the accounting department. It may be in respect of daily allowances, per diems, or things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, isn't that the CSB sending it up to the headquarters to have it dealt with?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go on to the next document, please. Or was that the last one? Yes, sorry, that was the last. Right. Can we go to, in the document, please, it's the -- no, can we go to page 10, please, in the document. 10th page. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: More payment documents, would you agree? Do you see there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. We are advised by the Court Officer that for technical reasons we must take the break now for a half hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Can I just finish this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you see there the payment being claimed, Mr. Orasanin, for the Konjic SJB, the Visegrad SJB, and the SJB Foca?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does Mr. Zecevic now accept that this is a claim for payment? Does Mr. Cvijetic now accept that?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't see a link with the witness's statement as to what he noticed in those SJBs. He didn't talk about money, whether there was a lack of money. He only spoke about the fact that CSB Trebinje, Trebinje staff never toured any of the stations and that they were left or that -- at least that they felt left out in the cold. And this is also in his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We'll take the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we have time at the end of today, I wonder if we could return to the question of timing all over as regards to the Zupljanin case. And I've been discussing matters with Mr. Krgovic and I think it may assist all of us if at least we can raise the situation with Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner. While the witness is on his way back to the stand, we have considered Mr. Zecevic's application for a delay for the reasons that he advanced. And bearing in mind that -- the witness that he has scheduled, that he would -- should, in all fairness, be allowed some time to deal with what may be new documents with which he has to consider, but bearing also in mind the fact that we are sitting afternoons next week and we are not scheduled to sit tomorrow, Monday being a holiday, so we would resume on Wednesday afternoon. We think that he should be allowed -- he may be allowed a day, which is Tuesday, and we would pick up on Wednesday with this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, what about letting us know whether -- who the witnesses are that he's going to drop? Are Your Honours going to give him a time on that one too?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, echoing Ms. Korner's request, it would be helpful, if you're so inclined, if you could do that as soon as you're able to. It would assist all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As I said, Your Honours, I will over the weekend and we will inform the Trial Chamber and the parties about our decision on Monday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tuesday, because Monday's not a working day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, in the course of your evidence --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, may I be excused because I need to inform the VWS --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In the course of your evidence on Monday, you told the Court that the places that you visited, and this is at page 21901, like Visegrad and Foca, Brcko, Rudo, Cajnice, the prosecutor's office wasn't functioning at all and neither was the court. I'd like you to have a look, please, at the prosecutor's log-book for Brcko. And you were visiting Brcko in May of 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's tab 1A and it's 65 ter 1537. Could it be -- I think it's easier if he has the printed-out copy. And, yes, it's 0615-2066. Page 8 in B/C/S. We've only got it in B/C/S; we don't have a translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Not terribly easy to see either on the screen or in the printed copy, but does that show a list of cases for May or partway through May? I don't know whether we can ... dates are not terribly easy --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just have a quick look through it, Mr. Orasanin, and just confirm that that shows cases being listed with dates in May, and I think you'll find it goes on over a number of pages. If we look at number --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we ... let's start with -- sorry, can we go back to page 4. I think that's the easiest. I think Your Honours will find it easier to find the dates. And can we have page 4 up on the screen. At the top you'll find 206 -- 0615-2062.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I should shown -- I should have given this to you last night. Can you -- all I'm asking you to do is have a quick look through, and can you confirm, Mr. Orasanin, that it appears that the prosecutor's office was, in fact, working through this period? That's all I'm asking you to do. Mr. Orasanin, I know that it's -- can you confirm that it does appear that the prosecutor's office was actually working? And, indeed, some of the clearest dates we can see are those in April, the rest, I'm afraid, are not so clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, just a moment. Here you can see that the year is 1993, that the prosecutor's office functioned in 1993, as far as I can tell.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Actually, no. I know it's -- I appreciate it's very difficult to see on the screen, but if you look at the page we're looking at, it's clearly 1992. Look at the continuation. Look at the third column, please. It's much, much clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's when documents were received. We heard testimonies to the effect that offices were open to receive documents. But if you look further in the right-hand side columns, you will see that the prosecutor's office actually started looking into cases and acting upon them only in 1993, at least this is what I can tell from the excerpt that is on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we've heard evidence about this in any event. I'm just, as I say, putting this document to Mr. Orasanin to see whether or not he wishes to change his assertion. If he doesn't, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, do you wish to change your assertion that the prosecutor's offices were not working? Mr. Orasanin?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I was saying about my report and what is contained in my report, this is what I told you about the municipalities of Foca, Rudo, Cajnice, and Visegrad. This is what we put in our report. We said that the prosecutor's office and the court were not organised. Our order to them was to prepare all the criminal reports, and they told us that all the doors were locked. In those municipalities, I'm 99 per cent sure that the prosecutor's offices and the courts did not function and --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... stop, stop, stop, Mr. Orasanin, please. I asked -- I agree, but you threw in Brcko, and I'm merely asking you whether you now wish to change your classification of Brcko as one where the prosecutor's office was not working?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were there on the 15th of May, no investigations were going on by the prosecutor's office or the court. The police could not carry out investigations because it is the prosecutor's office and the court that order the police to carry out investigations, hence the problem. That's why I concluded that they were not functioning. Pursuant to the Law on Criminal Procedure, the police cannot carry out any investigations until the moment the investigative judge and the prosecutor 's office issue their order to the crime investigating police. That's why I concluded that they were not operational.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Stop, stop, stop, stop, stop, please. Who told you in Brcko in your one-hour's visit that the prosecutor's office was not working?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spent an hour talking to Mr. Gavrilovic, Pero Gavrilovic; he was in charge of national security and the crime prevention service, as far as I can remember, and that was also within our purview. And later on I read some instructions pursuant to which he became the head of the crime prevention services. When we were there, there was a gap, a vacuum of sorts. Later on he was appointed the head of the crime prevention services, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Honest, Mr. Orasanin, I simply asked you: Who told you this? The answer was Mr. Gavrilovic. Full stop. Not what happened to him then or afterwards. Now, I simply want to ask you whether you wish to change your opinion, having seen that there was a prosecutor's office log-book being kept for cases at that time in respect of Brcko. Leave aside all the other places you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have just used a magnifying-glass to look at this log-book. And despite my best wishes, I simply cannot identify the dates that Ms. Korner has just referred to. And it is a big question whether the witness can answer Ms. Korner's questions the way they are put. The witness is testifying about the facts, about the situation that he found and the messages that he was conveyed, and I believe that his evidence should be restricted only to that, what he saw and what he was told and what problems he encountered. That's the kind of problems that he reported and conveyed. He was not in the prosecutor's office to see whether this is a log-book for 1992 and so on and so forth. I believe that we cannot go any further with this witness when it comes to interpreting the contents of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Whereas you're perfectly correct, Mr. Cvijetic, I suppose, in fairness to the witness, if Ms. Korner at the appropriate time wishes to remind the Chamber of apparent contradictions, she is allowing him the opportunity to speak to it. How far she wishes to go with this is a matter for her, but that's the purpose. But on principle, of course, it appears to me that you're correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, as I've made it clear the Defence on a number of occasions, I'm obliged to put my case to the witness. And our case is that his assertions over this are wrong. Your Honours, the best thing I can do is for the moment ask that the document be marked MFI because I think it's right that without getting -- there's no translation for it, in any event, and without getting better copies and a translation, but just so that we have it marked and then, if I may, I'd make the application to put it in. I know there's already been evidence about it, in any event, from the witness who came to talk about the prosecutor's log-books.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Marked, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pending translation and a full application to put it in, but just marking it for the moment so we know what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours, I don't see any grounds to introduce anything through this witness. Not even to mark it for identification. Who is going to interpret the document for us once this witness is gone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One more thing, Your Honours, if I may. On the list of the Prosecutor's witnesses when the Prosecutor presented its case, there were witnesses who could have testified about this document but they were withdrawn. How can we now interpret this document through this witness? How can we tender it and admit it if the witness that we are dealing with now is unable to say anything about it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, may I suggest you hold your fire until -- Ms. Korner's indicated she wants it marked pending both the translation and the full application to put it in. So may I suggest you hold your fire until she makes her full application. In the meantime, I suppose, so it doesn't get lost, we mark it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2353, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, let's deal with what you say about if no prosecutor's office was working, the police couldn't investigate. Are you asserting that once the police had put in a preliminary criminal report to the prosecutor's office they could do no more and indeed - well, let's deal with that one first, could do no more to investigate?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is the first time I hear of a preliminary criminal report. I have no idea what that might be. There is no such thing under our law.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Once the police had put in the criminal report, which is the first stage, to the prosecutor's office, is it your assertion that the police were prohibited from doing any further investigation until directed by the prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The police is duty-bound to collect information necessary to shed light on the criminal offence. But I said that the police cannot work without the approval of a judge and a prosecutor's office. I'm referring to investigative activities for which approval is required. But the police are duty-bound to collect information necessary to identify the perpetrator of a crime. But how do we do that without an on-site investigation? And the rule is that a good on-site investigation accounts for 50 per cent of the success in finding the perpetrator. That's what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That may or may not be the case, but, as I understand it, you do accept the police are duty-bound to carry on investigating to the extent that they can, if you like, without a prosecutor directing them.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept. But when we speak about serious crimes, murder and others, then special activities must be carried out and an on-site investigation must be performed. I think it was Article 154 of the Law on Criminal Procedure that the investigative magistrate orders the carrying out of investigative activities. That was a provision of the law. It has been changed meanwhile. So the investigative magistrate and the prosecutor could entrust these activities formerly but can no longer do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And indeed you yourself said that when you saw the cases in Doboj where there were unknown perpetrators in murder cases, you yourself said that there had to be a special force put together to investigate these cases, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I said that operative groups must be set up. And the events in Doboj that I saw in the log-book, there was also a register of on-site investigations. Members of the MUP carried out on-site investigations. Which is -- these are not mandatory for all crimes, but they are in case of serious crimes such as murder and some others. Whether the police got an approval from the investigative magistrate to go on site, I don't know, because it's the investigative magistrate who is in charge of these activities and the police only provides assistance. And here we saw that the on-site investigations were conducted and then we tasked our operatives to examine that. I may not be fully clear, but that's how we acted then. Nowadays, the crime detection service has smaller -- hasn't so a wide authority as before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry about nowadays or historical days. Right. Thank you. Now let's deal with these Doboj -- that was the one inspection that you concede was an inspection. Firstly, did you notify Doboj CSB and Doboj SJB in advance that you were coming to do the inspection? And that just requires "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a rule, to send a dispatch and information saying that the inspectors are coming. But if there are no communication lines ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, did you or didn't you? Or can't you remember? "Yes," "no," or "I can't remember"?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember. Maybe Nikola Milanovic did that because he wrote the -- these decisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You told the police in -- oh, police. You told the OTP in interview, in fact, on the topic of communications - and this is at page 51 of your interview - that -- you were -- in fact, you were being asked about reports, and you said that -- sorry, this is the bottom of page 50, you were being asked in April, May, up to, I don't know, September, let's say, about CSB sending reports, there were such obligations, but now whether they had technical possibilities to do so, I doubt it. They from Doboj could not send dispatch or information over here, but the centre should have -- was supposed to have that. You have this dispatch, and you were referring to -- went by courier. "Q. That's what I'm actually saying, that even though the communication was bad, there would always be possibility to send something through messenger, through a courier." And you said: "Yes, I suppose, during the first three months it was difficult, but traffic connections were cut, let alone telecommunication lines had not been established yet." So do you agree that couriers could be used even if telephone lines or radios were not working?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I know, I was saying in the context of the impossibility to travel by road. It wasn't possible to go there until early July. I'm unfamiliar with these facts. A courier must also travel by road. Only if they fly in a helicopter, then not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's deal with the content of your visit to Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, we see that you went to Doboj on the 14th of August, 1992, and the first thing, apparently, you did was have a meeting with the Doboj CSB and SJB public security operatives; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was on the 25th. That's when we were in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, that's what you say -- I know you say that, but did Mr. Minic do a meeting, an inspection, at Doboj with you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was Mr. Minic and Nikola Milanovic too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely. And it's hardly likely that he did a separate visit before that, is it? Indeed, well ...

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I remember, he went there on a number of occasions. There were mixed teams; uniformed police and operatives.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Well, let's see if this jogs your memory, shall we? You say you were there for two days, and this visit, as recorded, was two days. The following day --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There was this meeting at the Dom Milicije in Doboj; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, one meeting was held at the Dom Milicij e. It was a large meeting. But I seem to remember that Cedo Tosic was there, or somebody from the uniformed police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, what I want to ask you about is, was a discussion in the meeting that you were at about the monitoring of genocide and war crimes against the Serbian people, which you will see --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we move the bottom up slightly, the page, because it's quite difficult to see in B/C/S. Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was there such discussion?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember attending the meeting. Somebody was there, but I think it was Cedo Tosic, one of these --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, are you saying that Mr. Minic, Mr. Milanovic, and Mr. Tosic went to Doboj on the 14th and the 15th for two days and then you and Mr. Minic and Milanovic went back on the 24th? What would be the point of that? Well, firstly, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember attending the meeting at the Dom Milicije. I know that there was a meeting there, it was a large meeting, but I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, where were you? Where were you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a regional meeting there but, as far as I remember, another team went. They were representatives of the SJBs from the region, and it was a mixed team, as far as I know. That's what I know, what I remember. And that's what I say in my first -- said in my first statement. There was a question about the number and about someone coming from Derventa and Brod and such. The investigator asked me about it. But I'm sure I wasn't at that meeting. And there was discussion about war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Look. I'm sorry, Mr. Orasanin, I don't follow, now, what you're saying. You, Minic, Milanovic go off to Doboj to conduct what you say was really the only proper inspection that you did in August. Are you now saying that this record of this meeting at the Dom Milicije is a completely separate visit?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that we were at this meeting where the representatives of the SJBs of the region were present.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Look. Just stop --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that was at the Dom Milicije.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The record says this is a "meeting at the Dom Milicije in Doboj with the operative personnel on the territory of the Doboj CSB." It is a record, I can assure you -- well, right, never mind. I'll rephrase that question. Were you or were you not present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that I attended only the meeting in the Doboj building and we only spent the night at the Dom Milicije. It's possible that I know some of these things when we went to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Because, you see, you told us, when you were giving your evidence, that you had a short meeting with Mr. Bjelosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we just can through this to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was discussed there also was working and co-operating with the prosecutor's offices and courts in Doboj. Was there discussion at the meeting that you attended of co-operation with the prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that we visited Doboj. But that we initiated a meeting? We spoke to the president of the higher court there whose name was Sinisa, what was his last name? He's an attorney now. That was our initiative, and that's what I spoke about. And the prosecutor and they were presenting -- oh, now I remember the name: Sinisa Djordjevic. They were speaking about making sure that the accused is present at the proceedings. But whether he was present ... there may be some confusion, but I remember this: Sinisa Djordjevic was a president of the higher court or prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know, honestly, Mr. Orasanin, this is a discussion not with members of the prosecutor's office or whatever, but whether there was discussion at the police meeting about co-operation with the prosecutor's office. Now, do you recall that happening?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever we have a meeting, we make a snap-shot of the situation and discuss the co-operation between the police and the courts. This is our basic task. The job wouldn't be done if we hadn't reviewed these possibilities. It would have only been a half success. I remember what it says here, that the man spoke about the problems of the court and the prosecutor's office --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes, thank you, Mr. Orasanin. Thank you. I'm suggesting to you in the clearest possible terms, Mr. Orasanin, that that visit to Doboj was with you, Milanovic, Minic, Tosic, and yourself, the four of you went there. There weren't two visits to Doboj, there was just the one visit. And you were present at this meeting, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. You mentioned Tosic and our presence. I'm 1.000 per cent sure that we weren't there. Cedo Tosic never went with me. Actually, later, once we had seen that the problems were those of the uniformed police, we weren't authorised to do the work of the uniformed police because the problems were greater. And we said, Let's make a snap-shot of this and then we'll return to Bijeljina and then --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Leave Bijeljina, please, alone. We're talking about your full inspection of Doboj. And it was -- I'm sorry, it was either Cedomir Tosic or Radenko Vujicic.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radenko Vujicic, never. I state that with full responsibility. We're wasting time. I remember it as if it had been yesterday. I allow for the possibility of some confusion though. You mentioned Ostoja Minic. When there were investigations in 2005, I spoke to him about some things and I was trying to convince him that I was in Banja Luka with them. And he tried to convince me that I never went to Banja Luka, that it was just him and Nikola. And that's the truth. Because when we spoke to the investigators, I contacted Ostoja Minic by phone. These people we spoke about, it's not a secret. Anybody could know what we spoke about. That's the kind of man I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So do I understand this: That you and Mr. Minic in 2005 got together to discuss what you had been doing in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No need. We already discussed this topic. And whatever we did was very professional. And I'm sure that's the way they do things even now. And that's -- this is the way they worked earlier, when we speak about the team of Nikola Milanovic and the regions around Foca, Visegrad, and Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What makes you say it was the 24th of August that you went there and not the 18th?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, after that other teams went. After ten days, they went. There was a problem regarding the reserve police. The minister issued an order with this regard, and somebody told me to look into that as well. I don't know who it was. Maybe Macar or somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Where is the report of your full inspection on the 24th of August with Mr. Minic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was submitted to the administration and I believe that it was drafted by Nikola Milanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Listen, I'm asking you where it is.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the administration for crime prevention. And as for the mixed teams, that went -- the line that they followed was the department for crime prevention, then the administration for crime prevention. For example, Cedo Tosic, who is a uniformed inspector, he went with them. And I believe that they also attended the meeting, because the entire team attended the meeting, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I'm simply asking, did you keep a copy of that report, because the only report we have, apart from these notes of a meeting on the 18th -- the 14th and 15th of August at Doboj, is one that's in October?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were in Doboj, a report was drafted, stock was taken of the situation, and as far as I know and as far as I can tell Your Honours, that was done in a professional manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So your evidence is -- all right. Let's cut this short because I don't want to waste time on a document. You say you didn't go with Mr. Minic, and whoever else was there, and Milanovic on the 14th and 15th of August, you went separately on the 24th of August and conducted your inspection?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that there were three of us. I'm sure that there were three of us. We had a car. We had some problems with the authorisation --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes, no, I really --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and we were parked over in Brcko and I remember that because we had --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. That's your evidence, is it? Two visits, four -- according to this, and 24th. Now, just tell me how it is you're so sure it was the 24th? Do you have a diary for 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, the witness explained how he knows. He explained the link. He explained it during my examination, during yours as well, and he referred to that authorisation. And he mentioned several times how come he remembers that it was on the 24th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was shown Brcko -- the authorisation was issued in Brcko, and it was signed on Macar's behalf by Nikola, I believe, because in 1992 there were huge problems, official IDs were not valid, i.e., there were other people who carried them, so we had to have a piece of paper, a document. And I told you about those official IDs. When we were stopped by a soldier in uniform and he told us, I don't care about your official ID, I have one of them. And he showed us a blank ID that was the -- that was looted in a depot where they were kept --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... [Microphone not activated] ... yes, don't -- don't -- please, please don't tell us that whole story all over again.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this was all done by design. There was a design behind all that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Finally in this second visit -- [Microphone not activated] ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Ms. Korner, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You did on that occasion look at the books properly, did you? That is, the KU books?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First we had a meeting with the chief of the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... no, no, stop. Did you properly inspect the books, the KU books? First the CSB and of the SJB?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the three of us, one of us, I believe it was Nikola, looked at the KU books of the CSB. And as for the log-book of events for a uniformed police station, it's a general book where everything is registered, including breaches of discipline, traffic violations, and other incidents. That may have been the origin of the problem because the uniform --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... stop, stop. Did you - and by "you" I mean you personally - look at any of the books?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I didn't look at the KU book in the public security station. I don't remember that anybody in the course of our visit -- because for that we would have had a uniformed inspector with us. That's why we wanted to do it more thoroughly the following time. There were problems regarding the functioning of the uniformed police and what the uniformed policemen do. And as for the KU books ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, I understood this was your great big proper visit, sorry, inspection. Are you now saying that you ignored the inspection checklist and did not, any of you, inspect the KU books? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
