utterances.text: No, no, no. I was putting things in the perspective of all the other inspection visits, and I said that we did the best as we could. And I guarantee you that we took a snap-shot of the situation as it was. We saw that there were 10 or 11 killings and we based on shedding light on the crimes committed by unknown perpetrators. This is what we started. We ordered that operative groups should be set up in order to elucidate all the crimes. We established contact with the president of the second instance court. We also spoke to the chief of the crime prevention services --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Orasanin, this will not do. Stop. I'm not asking for a list of what you did. I'm simply asking you whether you inspected the KU books and you're saying no you didn't. Now, does that -- right.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- one of us did. Either Nikola or Ostoja did that. The rest of us, we looked at the cases and we talked to the chief of the crime prevention services who was in charge. We analysed cases. Of course we saw the register of those crimes and then we wanted to see what they were doing with that regard. That was that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Stop. Thank you. Last night you had a look at a copy of the Doboj SJB book. Did you yourself inspect that at the time, in August 1992? Yes or no? That's all. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know and all you can see in the report, I saw in there. I don't know whether I saw it myself or Ostoja did. I don't know. But it was a team-work. So all the killings are registered and what we saw tallies what that, and this is 1.000 per cent correct and sure. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. The second book, had you seen that one before? Let me show it to you again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which is 20102, tab 14 -- 40.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just -- just -- all I want to know is whether you saw that book at the time. I don't want to describe it for various reasons. Did you see that book? Did you see that book?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the three of us did. However, when I looked at what was going on, we registered all that, I can see that everything is registered, that 10 or 11 killings by unknown perpetrators, I remember some names, some on on-site inspections were carried out, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Stop. Just tell us what that book is, please. I want you to tell us what that book is.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a register or a log-book of perpetrated crimes. They are all there. All the gravest crimes are registered in here, and I mean the crimes that were inspected and investigated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it a CSB book or is it an SJB book, Doboj?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says CSB here. However, I don't know whether you'll be able to understand me. What it says here, serious crimes for which there are on-site inspections, in the bigger centre there are two services. The crime prevention service has its own duty officer. That's how it was done before the war, and it all depends on the internal organisation of the service.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I know that. I simply want to know - and there is a reason for me asking you this - does that appear to --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just, please. -- does that appear to be a log-book maintained by the CSB or the SJB Doboj?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that these are on site inspections which are registered at the centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but I think you're -- are you reading -- what are you reading there? Are you reading the thing at the top? Yes, well -- no, I don't want you to read that. I know that's what it says. But that's not on the book itself. I want you -- from looking at the book, whether you can tell me whether this is CSB or SJB. If you can't, then please say so. Leave aside the yellow piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, this shows inspections that were carried out following crimes, so this is probably the centre log-book.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you very much. Right you can hand that back.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, may I also --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, you mayn't. Just give it back to me, please. All right. Finally, on the Doboj, can I ask you to look, please, at 1D542, which is tab 36A of our bundle. That's a list of the unknown perpetrators cases that you were talking, is that right, from Doboj, Mr. Orasanin?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Can you confirm that each and every one of the victims of -- sorry, just a moment. Yes, sorry. Yes, that all of the victims - I just want to check this - appear to be non-Serb victims?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the names. I found them in the log-book.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. They're all non-Serbs, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 1 --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In fact, they're pretty well all Muslims, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... don't count them.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are 10. Ten.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Are all the victims of these crimes, which are the only non -- unknown perpetrator crimes, they're all non-Serb, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, please don't interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you allow the witness to read the document. That's my remark at this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understood this was a document he'd seen, particularly as it's a Defence document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document? I've not seen the document before. This is the first time I see it. I remember the names. These names are in the KU book --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Are they all non-Serb names? That's all. That's all I want you to confirm.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, here. But in the KU book I found 12 murders; among those, victims are also Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to ask you to allow the witness to read the last part where it says with regard to the above report and where it says who the victims are. Why don't you allow the witness to read the document through? Please, can you read and see if there are also Serb victims in here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number 8. From 1 through 8 I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the last number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then you don't have the entire document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there you go. Are you reading from the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, from 1 through 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, could you please ask the usher to provide the witness with a hard copy of the document so that the witness can read it through. I don't care for these examination methods. Could you please read the document until the very end. The last part, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could we have the next page on the screen, please, in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the last part, where it says "in connection with the above report" ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see this is it. Uh-huh. "In connection with the above report"; do you want me to read this?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know, Your Honour, I'm sorry, I'm taking exceeding objection to this. This is -- all of this can be dealt with in re-examination. This is not a proper way for Defence counsel to behave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And it's prolonging the proceedings. Mr. Cvijetic, let Ms. Korner formulate her questions. And if the question is unfair, we will intervene. But let's get on with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Orasanin, you've had a chance to read through this. These are the names you yourself saw in the KU books. They are the 11 unsolved, unknown perpetrator cases; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, crimes committed by unknown perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Of the 11 names of the crimes committed by unknown perpetrators, are any of those names Serb names, the victims?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we -- I don't know what Your Honour -- I've forgotten what time the break is in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It's in three minutes' time. But if it's convenient, we can take it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm just going to deal, very briefly, with Banja Luka, which was the last place he visited. And that's the end of the inspection -- of this lot of inspections. Or, Your Honour -- I'm in Your Honour's hands, I don't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Do you still expect to finish this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, so we'd take the break now and come back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, just before the -- while the witness is being brought - thank you - can I make it clear that over the adjournment we've had another look at the Brcko book. It runs until roughly the end of April, then there's an underlining. It is 1992. But the next entry after April is not until the 1st of July. So I should make that absolutely clear. So the point I was trying to make was that it was operating in May. There's nothing to show that it was, in that book. And I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. So noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have looked at the book together and noticed that, so the issue has been resolved.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, you told the Court that after Doboj you went to Banja Luka CSB. And you spent there -- this is at page 21920 of the transcript and goes on to 21921, you reviewed the crimes log-book, criminal complaints, and so on and so forth. Do you remember telling the Court that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we came to Banja Luka --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, that's all I need. That's what happened, was it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you also spend only one hour in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Where is your report on this inspection?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a single report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So there was a report on Doboj --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Doboj, Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- and Banja Luka. Right. Again, can you explain why you and Mr. Minic and Milanovic were doing an inspection in late August, around the 25th it must have been according to you, when there had been an earlier inspection on the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we have a look, please, at P631, tab 28. Report on the performed inspection of the CSB and public security stations in the territory of the Autonomous Region Krajina. Can we go to the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We'll see the 5th of August, report submitted by Sreto Gajic, department chief, and Mr. Mirosavic, police inspector.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we can see that in the report. They are inspectors of the uniformed police, as far as I remember. Tomislav Miroslavic [as interpreted] and Sreto Gajic. They are from that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why was there an inspection being done within a matter of weeks by you, Mr. Minic, and Milanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were in Doboj and finished the work there, and then we went to Banja Luka about crime. And this is probably an inspection of the uniformed police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What, do you mean you went there of your own initiative, on your own initiative, rather than having been told to go there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, these inspectors were there to make a snap-shot of the uniformed police. The same as us who went to Doboj. And then the need became obvious to conduct an inspection of the uniformed police. That follows from some work duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Thank you, that's all I want to ask you. Now, Visegrad and Foca, your visit, for which you wrote a report that we looked at with the Defence, but I just want to understand this: Is it your assertion that Visegrad was not operating properly; or was it, apart from the shortage of staff which we looked at, a properly operating SJB?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We found out and stated in the report, after visiting Rudo, we came to Visegrad, we were also there briefly. I said that those were short visits and our first visits to that area. We started at Foca and finished at Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Stop, please. Answer the question. Is it your contention that Visegrad was not a properly functioning SJB?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it may be good to show the witness his report for Visegrad to jog his memory and then he can answer. That may be useful.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He's just looked at it. I want to know whether he makes --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, I want to know, Mr. Orasanin, whether you make the same complaints, that there were insufficient staff or that things were not being done properly at Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were problems there, just as in all those stations, problems with the prosecutor's office and the court, problems with conducting on-site investigations and investigative activities and everything that was necessary. That's what we found out, because without that the service cannot function. That was our goal. And they -- there were plans for other inspectors to go there later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. It's not, however, that there were insufficient police officers at -- on duty, is it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember now how many police officers in uniform were there and how many crime enforcement officers. I remember that there were three or four in crime enforcement. But we were told that there were -- they were fewer than before. But as far as I know, there were plans for going to Visegrad again to assess the situation. I know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, no doubt you're aware of the house fire that was started and that has been the subject of trials at this court in Visegrad which took place in June or July, I think maybe July, of 1992. When you examined the KU books at Visegrad, did you find any record of that crime?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were in Visegrad, we stayed an hour. There were talks, and we noticed that. But the problem was with the investigative activities. When we returned, I know that there were plans for Milanovic maybe, or somebody from our group, to go there again because there was talk about some corpses. That's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Are you saying that you did not examine the crime registers in Visegrad? That -- just say "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there were three or four inspectors but they were absent.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Look, did you or did you not - and by "you," I mean you or either Mr. Minic or Mr. Milanovic - look at the KU books?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's stated in the report, but I don't remember it now. Probably one of us did. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, all right. Let's have a look at the report because there's no reference in the report to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have up, please, it's P6 -- oh, no. It's tab 29 in the Defence bundle, and I think it must be 33 -- no, it's 1D53 -- sorry. 33D1. 1D571.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's tab 29 in the -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we go to the second page, please, in --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to ask the usher to hand this binder with the exhibits to the witness. It may be easier for him to read the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, what you say there is there's a crime prevention department with three employees, criminal reports by injured parties have been, I think it must be filed, and a number have been processed. So does that mean you looked at the criminal reports themselves or the KU register? Mr. Orasanin?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: A presentation was made about the crimes committed and the problems of the prosecutor's office and that the criminal report were not filed with the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Stop, stop. I can read that, so can everybody else. Did you or did you not look at the KU books?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we were briefed at the meeting that we attended and this is what we noted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Stop, stop. I'm not going to go on with this. In the report you talk about: "In the Visegrad area there have been cases of murder, that is, genocide, committed against Serbs." No reference at all to - let's use your word - genocide committed against non-Serbs, Muslims, is there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember this, when we were there, somebody brought a cassette because communications were down. And that's why this was put here. We were supposed to give it to the news agency. And this was a recent crime, as far as I remember, in a village, maybe Jelasice. Because it was so recent, this remark was made here. And I know that another trip to Visegrad was planned for a later time in order to -- in order to collect information, because there was a mention of corpses in the Drina. Jelasice, yes, that's the name of the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... it says the corpses in the Drina -- stop. The corpses in the Drina weren't related to anything to do with the fires that killed all those people or the people who were shot by the river. They were to do with crimes against the Serbs, were they?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now what?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may have a moment, how can the witness answer this question? He must first be asked whether he was aware of that crime. The Prosecutor is basically giving evidence about what we have heard in this trial. The Prosecutor is skipping several steps before asking the witness this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I was actually asking the witness, and that's how I started off, whether there was any mention of that to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So do we take it from that that either it was never mentioned to you or you -- well, first of all, was it mentioned to you by the Visegrad police that in June deliberate fires had been set which had killed large numbers of extended Muslim families?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't know it then. I know that there were some activities, there was a dispatch, it may have been sent by the chief, about some groups over there, and para-groups, but only when we returned. Some sort of problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What, the Lukic brothers?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief -- the station chief wrote that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Isn't it right that - and I'm going to come on to that as the final topic, Mr. Orasanin - the only interest that the MUP, from the top to the bottom, had in investigating was crimes that were committed against Serbs, and that's why this paragraph appears in this way?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said why this remark was made. And the colleagues who were with me also know. Because of that cassette which was --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes, yes, you told us -- don't tell us about the cassette again. All right, you don't agree with my suggestion. When did you learn about the house fires, then, please?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember now. I believe that there was some sort of report or dispatch from the station chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but when?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's why -- but I was soon transferred to another position in the border police and so now I can't --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, you weren't trans -- no, stop, stop, stop, stop. You weren't transferred until November 1992. Was -- that report from the SJB chief on the house fires and other crimes committed against non-Serbs, was that before you went to the border police?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I remember, some reports were there in July. I can't remember now. It may have been later, after I was transferred. But I know that there was talk about another team going there again, that some corpses had been found in the Drina. I know that from when they returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Corpses of what, Serbs or non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We don't know that. But I know that they should go there again. And I think they were non-Serbs, where -- when we were in Bijeljina, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When what? When, you mean, the MUP was in Bijeljina? The headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, look, it can't be -- you say it was either in July 1992 or November 1992 after you left. Presumably after you had gone to the border police --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, just pause. -- that you heard about the house fires. If you had gone to the border police in November 1992, then you would hardly likely have seen a report from the SJB chief, would you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember now, you know, if a report reached the administration. But the headquarters was in Bijeljina --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... look, stop.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means the crime prevention administration was in Bijeljina. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I don't -- the -- you, when you went to the border police, no longer saw reports intended for the crime prevention unit, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reports are passed on along the lines of work. And some contain information intended for the analyses department and also for the media. I don't know and understand what you're asking.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... no. Please, please, Mr. Orasanin, stop. This is going on forever. When you went to the border police, you no longer saw reports from an SJB chief in Visegrad about killings, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If it was a dispatch, if a dispatch was sent out --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Honestly, Mr. Orasanin, this is -- just answer this, please. We take it, therefore, that the report on those killings from Visegrad must have come before you went to the border police?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the witness should be asked whether he's sure at all that such a report came in. I cannot conclude from his answers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... for re-examination, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, that's disgraceful. You cannot help the witness out like this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I'll try one last time and then I want to finish as quickly as I can, Mr. Orasanin. You told us you thought the report arrived in July but it could have been after you left. You would not have seen this report, would you, once you were in the border police? That's all I want to know. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember a report about paramilitary groups there which was from July or so. The station sent out such a report. But who -- I don't remember who the suspects are or who the victims were. But there were some problems with paramilitaries who were active there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did that report on paramilitaries include --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, don't answer. Did that report on the paramilitaries include an account of the appalling crimes they had committed against non-Serbs; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have been sent by dispatch, or perhaps that was information from the media. It was long ago. I simply don't remember. But it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's fine, stop. Foca, I just want to deal with one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, before you move to somewhere else. Mr. Orasanin, the house fire, as Ms. Korner calls it, is a quite massive and important incident, that's right, isn't it? You know that now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now then, let's take it that when doing the inspection you did in Visegrad, you didn't know about it, and your colleagues who were with you to do an inspection did not know about it, nevertheless - and this is my question, and I would like to have a short answer to that - wouldn't it anyhow have been told or been found out by you that this happened and wouldn't it have been mentioned in your report, a report that dates from one month after the event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, had we known that, we certainly would have mentioned it in the report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I know, I know, I know. But my question is: Wouldn't the people in Visegrad you were inspecting, weren't they under the obligation to tell you about this? Or if not, weren't they under the obligation to have that logged in one or the other log-book where you should have found it or could have found it? But it wasn't there. You inspected the books, it wasn't there, because you don't know about it. Because if you had known, you would have mentioned it. So my question is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you agree with me that they should have told you, that they should have told you, or that you -- that it would have been normal and the -- their obligation to file that in one way or the other in one or the other log-book that you were inspecting, but they didn't, is that it? That's how I interpret, now, your "yes." Am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If we had known that those things had happened, we would have mentioned that in the report. Either if we had been briefed or if we had found it ourselves in the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I want you to look, please, at -- [Microphone not activated]. Sorry, I'd like you to look, please, at a document which is 65 ter 10395, tab 30 of our binder. This is a report, 10th of August, 1992. At the top it says "Cedo Tosic and Vojin Vukovic." Are those two of the inspectors that you worked with?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not belong to the crime prevention administration. They did not belong to our administration. However, I remember that they were in the area of Herzegovina, I believe. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So you wouldn't be able to identify their signatures?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not work with them. I worked in the administration for crime prevention and they worked in the police administration. Cedo Tosic also carried out inspection in the territory of Doboj. I've already mentioned that. He actually went on one inspection to inspect the reserve police force, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes. I don't think I can take that further. Thank you. Right. Can I deal now, please, with your assertion that the MUP investigated war crimes whosoever they were committed against. I've already suggested to you that the only interest the MUP had in investigating war crimes was those that were allegedly against Serb victims. Could you have a look, please, at P173, which is at tab 9A. On the 16th of May, Mico Stanisic issued this order to the Security Services Centre and so ordered that "for the purpose of monitoring combat operations and regular activities of the organs of the interior, and in order to collect documentation on the crimes against the Serbian population," et cetera, et cetera. Were you aware of this order?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this was drafted when we were on our inspection in Podrinje, sometime in mid-May.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So you were aware of this order?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. Maybe we were travelling at that time. Perhaps. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the last page? Can we show the witness the signature to see whether it is, indeed, Mico Stanisic's order? Let's see who signed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, I didn't understand that there was any dispute that this was an order issued by Mico Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to see whether the witness recognises Mico Stanisic's signature on this document. This is all I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't imagine -- sorry, can we go back --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you aware of this order issued by Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I was probably on sick leave and later on I learned about that. Because we had had that accident, you know, I was absent for some ten days or so, you know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's fine. You learned about it later, but the --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I can't remember because I was on sick leave. We had had that accident, so I was at home until the end of May, so I don't --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, you said that. Stop. Did you learn -- you told us you learned about it later.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure because it was only sometime around the 28th of May. I was at home before that, so it would not make much sense for me to know. It wouldn't have been logical, would it? I don't know. I don't think that I've ever seen this before. This is a document about military activities and operations. This is what it's about, combat activities and operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, please, Mr. Orasanin, I just want an answer to this question: Whether you knew about the order on the 16th of May or whether you discovered it later, did you know that he had issued an order to the CSBs to collect documentation on war crimes committed against Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Never heard that? Oh, never mind. I think that's a mistake to ask that.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see this at the crime prevention administration, I'm sure, after my return from sick leave. I'm not familiar with this at all. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally, on this point --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was another document about war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I know there was. I want you to --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't -- I was -- I thought that that was the one, but it's not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Don't go on talking. Are you saying that you never understood that the concentration of the MUP was to get evidence about war crimes committed against Serbs? Did you never understand that was the object? No --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. I'd like you to look, please --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd like you to look please -- stop talking.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I would like you to look, please, at the MUP report for 1992, which is P625, at tab 37A. And can we go, please -- do you see this is a report April to December 1992 for -- of the Republika Srpska Ministry of the Interior. Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I would have to look at the contents first. I was an inspector at that time and not all documents reached me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Didn't all inspectors get a copy of the report of the work of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have our own reports, our own administration. We draft our own programmes and reports connected with our own administration, and I suppose that this was only seen by our bosses, by our managers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness needs to be shown the date when this report was compiled. And then it will be easier for him to answer whether he ever saw it and when.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It is very difficult to understand the witness, especially if the witness and the counsel are overlapping.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not in the MUP centre at the time. From December 1992 I was working on the setting up of the border police and I was not in the MUP at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want you to look, nonetheless, in respect of your answer about the interest that you had in investigating war crimes, at the part that deals with crime detection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In English that is page 12. And in B/C/S, page 13. No, must be -- sorry, that's not the page in B/C/S. It should say F120-1292 on the top. Yes, that's it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that the section headed "Crime Prevention and Detection"?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So that's the section that dealt with the work of your department; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the previous year, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yep, I quite agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now let's go, please, to - one, two - three pages on, page 15 in English. And it's - one, two, three - four pages on in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you see the paragraph in B/C/S that begins "in this period ..."?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. "In this period, the criminal inspectors"; that's you, isn't it, Mr. Orasanin? You were a criminal inspector?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "... visited all CSBs and SJBs and had meetings where they gave instructions for carrying out concrete operative activities. The focus of operative work in the CSBs and SJBs was on detection, documenting, and reporting members of the enemy army who had committed acts of genocide against the Serbian people, torched or destroyed immovable property, cultural, religious monuments, and other assets." Do you agree that is an accurate description of what the main task was?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree. This is not the style that the -- a criminal -- a crime prevention administration would have used. This is done by the analytical service. This is not a task of the crime prevention administration. It must have been somebody from the analytical service who did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to intervene. If such a voluminous report is shown to the witness in short batches and if it's given to the witness who has not seen it before, we are never going to get an adequate response. In the entire report there is information to which Ms. Korner refers and that is crimes against humanitarian and international law. There is even a chapter on that, but that chapter has not been shown to the witness. I believe that the method that Ms. Korner has used in examining this witness is not adequate because she is taking things out of the context. There is a whole report about the most serious types of crimes, and the question arises whether this witness is at all competent to comment upon the report that he has never seen. I've seen it and I had time to read it; whereas he has never seen it, he has never read it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, as I understand the import of Ms. Korner's question, it is -- although the witness himself, as he said, hasn't seen -- didn't see the report previously, it deals with an area -- it reports on matters for which he, according to his testimony, had responsibility, and he is merely being asked to comment on what is in the sections of the report. So I don't know that he needs to digest the whole of the report in order to answer the particular questions that are being phrased, that are being put to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, he cannot answer if he doesn't digest the entire report that concerns the work of his administration --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, unless I misunderstand what's been going on, he isn't asked -- being asked to do a commentary on this report. What he is asked, what is being put to him, is specific findings or sections of the report and asking for his -- what his reaction is to it because the report deals with areas for which he was responsible. Seems to be quite straightforward.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is absolutely right. The interruptions that Mr. Cvijetic is making either display his complete ignorance of the role of counsel when cross-examination is going on or are deliberately designed to try and help his witness. Either way, they are improper, and Your Honour has summarised the point that I'm trying to make.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this part, Mr. Orasanin, says that the criminal inspectors, and you've agreed you were one of them, visited the CSBs and SJBs, and the focus of your work, says the report, was dealing with members of the enemy army, as they're described, who committed acts of genocide against the Serbian people. I asked you whether you agreed with that assessment and you tell us you do not; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not, because we made questionnaires for both -- both to be processed. And there was a criminal report where there was a crime committed that we treated as murder, although it may have been a war crime. There is a general remark in the report, but I don't think that this was made on behalf of the crime detection and prevention service. We didn't have a position toward that. We had RZ and RZ1 forms, and we were instructed to fill in these forms for Serbs and for the others. That was our position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somebody wrote this who did not use the style that we used in our service.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, stop, stop. Right. I understand you don't agree. See, let me make it quite clear to you what our position is, Mr. Orasanin. I suggest to you that these forms and any orders allegedly looking to investigate war crimes against all manner of persons are no more than window-dressing and that all the Serbian MUP in Bosnia was interested in investigating was crimes committed against Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. Are these final arguments now or a question to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's -- I want to make quite clear what we suggest is the reality about these forms that you helped prepare. Do you agree or disagree? And you can say you agree or disagree.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree because we made them to be used. Minister Stanisic wrote a dispatch which was forwarded through the analyses department, and we in our administration actually made them. That's how we were brought up, irrespective of the events, and that's how it will always be. And if you're counting me in this group, then I take it as an offence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Finally, you said that the local authorities, the Crisis Staffs, effectively controlled the police. Were you aware of the instructions issued by the SDS party on the 19th of December, 1991, on the composition of Crisis Staffs? And you can just answer that "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes and no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes or no. Did you know about the instructions?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you know about the further instructions issued by Prime Minister Djeric on the 26th of April, 1992, about the work of Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it kind of. But during the war we had no time to think what -- who was planning what and the like. I was -- I spoke about that altogether already. Until the war we mostly dealt with detention cases, and that's why the confusion arose with regard to the Law on Internal Affairs --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop. And I'm sorry I'm interrupting the translation. Did you know that Prime Minister Djeric issued instructions on the composition and work of Crisis Staffs on April 26th, 1992; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember. I said what I know and what has to do with the judiciary and the MUP. That's what I followed, the legal procedure in these areas. And I said that I had these decisions on the establishment of courts and prosecutor's offices, and there's also something about prison facilities and something like that. And we were carrying that around with us and we were drivers and couriers and everything else. That's what I know. I was never interested in politics.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you did not know that those orders from the government said that the head of the MUP in a particular area had to be on the Crisis Staff? Answer "yes" or "no," please.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, how long do you expect you would be with your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that's what I was about to say. I think there's no point to try and deal with any one topic in the remaining ten minutes because for my re-examination I will need at least one session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's one matter as to timing which we could -- sorry, not timing, but the scheduling of the case, which Mr. Krgovic and I were discussing which we could just, perhaps, deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So, Mr. Orasanin, we are about to rise, but we have some housekeeping matters with which to deal. So the Chamber is not rising immediately, but you are now excused. We will resume the trial, when we adjourn, to 9.00 tomorrow morning and we will be in Courtroom I. So the usher will escort you from the courtroom while we continue those scheduling matters to which counsel have alluded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, having in mind what Mr. Zecevic said today with regard to the possible giving up on to two Defence witnesses, my estimate and the Bench's estimate that the Zupljanin Defence will begin its case after the break is unrealistic now. So probably -- probably the Zupljanin Defence will begin its case -- will open its case before the summer recess. I would like to remind the Trial Chamber of a few matters, namely our submission for approval of a 92 bis witness, which has not yet been replied to, and our submission to introduce a witness under Rule 92 quater. Only then we can make a final estimate of the time required and the sequence of calling witnesses for which we need Your Honours' ruling. But, at any rate, I will continue to fine-tune our list with the Prosecution. Certainly it will be required, as it will probably be earlier than expected, once the Stanisic Defence case finishes, we will need about a week to begin to call witnesses for the Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I know that counsel probably are tempted to think that they're being fobbed of when they give reminders to the Chamber about outstanding rulings, and the Chamber's response is that those rulings are well advanced. But I can say, about 92 bis and the 92 quater rulings, that they are well advanced in terms of the -- their being ready for delivery.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's more this: If the Zupljanin -- sorry, the Stanisic Defence drop two of their witnesses, as appears to be the case, the likelihood, working out the timing, is that their case would end at the end of the first week of July, which I think takes us up to the 9th -- yes, Friday the 9th of July. If Mr. Krgovic's application for a week is right, and this is what we're really asking, his case would start on the 18th -- Monday, the 18th of July, which would leave one week before the recess. We don't object to that if Your Honours are happy with the week off, it seems to us not an unreasonable request, to have a week between the two cases. I don't know if Mr. Krgovic intends to open his case or which witnesses he intends to call, so it would -- we would certainly ask that Your Honours make an order that we get, A, firstly whether he's going to open his case, and, two, the order of witnesses within the next week or so, so that we can organise our cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, we share the view that the request is not unreasonable, but we aren't going to rule on it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The observation that I would make is that having regard to what I said earlier about not picking this up again until the 29th of August, the unfortunate effect is going to be that the rhythm is going to be lost. But I suppose that's the nature of the exercise. But counsel would bear in mind that break and conduct -- arrange their witnesses accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I understand. And, of course, I'm not holding Mr. Krgovic to this at all, that he would intend to start with his expert, which would probably fit -- if he doesn't open his case, which would probably fit nicely into the week. Because his estimate is six hours, so that would take us just over a first day and cross would certainly be completed. He's not as long as the police expert or anything like that. So anyhow, Your Honours, I appreciate you weren't going to rule. We thought it right, however, that Your Honours had an opportunity to think about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Of course. Thank you. So we take the adjournment to 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 10th day of June, 2011, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.55 p.m.,
